milestones.title: Fustat founded
milestones.detail: After the Babylon Fortress fell in April 641, Amr ibn al-As founded a garrison town and capital beside it, with Egypt's first mosque. Historians trace present-day Cairo to this settlement.
milestones.source: Raymond (1993), Le Caire, pp. 13-18; Kennedy (2007), p. 161, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Fustat_and_other_early_Islamic_settlements

milestones.title: Abbasids found al-Askar
milestones.detail: The new Abbasid rulers laid out their own quarter north-east of Fustat as the provincial capital.

milestones.title: Ibn Tulun founds al-Qata'i
milestones.detail: Ahmad ibn Tulun built a new capital north-east of al-Askar with a palace, parade ground, hospital and aqueduct; his great mosque was built in 876-879. The Abbasids razed the city in 905, sparing the mosque.
milestones.source: Swelim (2015), Ibn Tulun: His Lost City and Great Mosque, pp. 32-37, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Fustat_and_other_early_Islamic_settlements

milestones.title: Fatimids found al-Qahira
milestones.detail: The general Jawhar laid out a fortified palace-city north-east of Fustat, with the al-Azhar Mosque. The caliph al-Mu'izz arrived in 973 and gave the city the name from which 'Cairo' derives.
milestones.source: Glasse & Smith (2003), The New Encyclopedia of Islam, p. 96, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Foundation_and_expansion_of_Cairo_under_the_Fatimids

milestones.title: Badr al-Jamali rebuilds the city walls
milestones.detail: The Fatimid vizier Badr al-Jamali rebuilt and extended the city walls in 1087. During his tenure (1073-1094) richer families from Fustat were first allowed to move into the palace-city.

milestones.title: Fustat set on fire
milestones.detail: The vizier Shawar burned unfortified Fustat to keep it from the Crusader king Amalric. The city survived but began a long decline as Cairo took over its trade.
milestones.source: Daly & Petry (1998), The Cambridge History of Egypt, vol. 1, p. 213, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Foundation_and_expansion_of_Cairo_under_the_Fatimids

milestones.title: Saladin begins the Citadel
milestones.detail: Saladin began the Citadel, seat of government until the 19th century, and a 20 km wall to enclose both Cairo and Fustat.

milestones.title: Mamluks take power
milestones.detail: Under the Mamluk sultans (1250-1517) building pushed the city outward; it reached its medieval peak of close to half a million people around 1340.
milestones.source: Raymond (1993), Le Caire; Shillington (2005), Encyclopedia of African History, p. 199, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Further_expansion_and_decline_under_the_Ayyubids_and_Mamluks

milestones.title: Black Death
milestones.detail: The plague reached Cairo in 1348 and returned more than fifty times before 1517. The first waves are estimated to have killed about 200,000 people.
milestones.source: Byrne (2004), The Black Death, pp. 104-105; Shoshan (2002), p. 4, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Further_expansion_and_decline_under_the_Ayyubids_and_Mamluks

milestones.title: Ottoman conquest
milestones.detail: Selim I conquered Egypt and reduced Cairo from an imperial capital to a provincial one; it remained the second city of the Ottoman Empire.

milestones.title: French occupation
milestones.detail: Napoleon's army occupied a city of fewer than 300,000 people from 1798 until the French surrender on 22 June 1801.
milestones.source: Winter (1992), Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule, pp. 226-227; Sicker (2001), p. 103, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#Ottoman_rule

milestones.title: Isma'il Pasha's new city
milestones.detail: Khedive Isma'il (r. 1863-1879) laid out a Paris-inspired quarter of squares and avenues west of the old city, now Downtown Cairo, with gas lighting and an opera house.

milestones.title: British occupation
milestones.detail: British forces occupied Egypt in 1882. Between 1882 and 1937 the built-up area grew from 10 to 163 square kilometres.

milestones.title: Heliopolis and Garden City begun
milestones.detail: The Heliopolis Oasis Company built a new suburb ten kilometres from the centre, and Garden City and Zamalek were developed in the same years.

milestones.title: Cairo Fire
milestones.detail: Riots known as the Cairo Fire or Black Saturday destroyed nearly 700 shops, cinemas, casinos and hotels in the downtown area.

milestones.title: Nasr City launched
milestones.detail: A large state-sponsored extension to the east officially began in 1959 and was mainly built in the mid-1970s.

milestones.title: Desert new towns programme
milestones.detail: The New Urban Communities Authority was set up to build satellite cities on desert land around Cairo. In the same year Historic Cairo became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

milestones.title: Cairo Metro opens
milestones.detail: The first line of the Cairo Metro began operating on 27 September 1987.

milestones.title: Cairo earthquake
milestones.detail: An earthquake in 1992 caused 545 deaths, injured 6,512 and left about 50,000 people homeless.
milestones.source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/view/hazards/earthquake/event-more-info/5339 , via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo#After_1956

milestones.title: New Administrative Capital announced
milestones.detail: Plans for a new capital in the desert 45 km east of Cairo were announced on 13 March 2015; its Iconic Tower was completed in 2024.

notes: Start date: the site has three candidate beginnings. (1) A trading post called Babylon is first mentioned in 50 BCE and the Roman Babylon Fortress, dated by excavation to Diocletian (c. 300 CE), still stands in Old Cairo; (2) Fustat was founded beside the fortress in 641; (3) the walled city of al-Qahira, which gives Cairo its name, was founded in 969. The file starts at Fustat in 641, following Abu-Lughod and Raymond, who trace present-day Cairo to it: it is the first foundation of a city (rather than a fort) on the site, it was the capital of Egypt, and Chandler's and Modelski's Cairo series begin with it. The fortress was partly deserted before the conquest and is treated as a predecessor. Ancient Memphis and Heliopolis lie inside today's metropolis but were separate cities. Population: figures to 1750 are Chandler's (one Modelski point for 700) and describe the whole agglomeration of Fustat, al-Askar, al-Qata'i and al-Qahira, not the walled city alone. There is no figure for 641-700. The decline after 1348, the long Ottoman-era low and the recovery are recorded as the sources give them; Shoshan's 15th-century range (150,000-300,000) is lower than Chandler's. Census figures from 1882 are for the Cairo governorate/city, not Greater Cairo, so Giza is excluded; the 1882 figure is disputed between 374,000 and 347,000 and the 1927 and 1937 figures could only be found rounded. Landmarks: structures older than 641 are left out because the timeline starts then; this excludes the Giza pyramids (c. 2560 BCE, inside the metropolis) and the Babylon Fortress. No sourced height could be found for the Mosque of Ibn Tulun (879), al-Azhar Mosque (972), Bab Zuwayla and Bab al-Futuh (1087-92), the Citadel, the Qalawun complex or al-Rifa'i Mosque, so they are omitted; the surviving medieval heights are minaret or wall heights from Wikipedia and are marked estimated. The Iconic Tower stands in the New Administrative Capital, which may fall outside the UN agglomeration boundary.
